title: Tax-owned data layer joining ERP and ledger data into one reconciled source
problem: Tax teams sit downstream of finance systems and often get aggregated data stripped of detail; EY's survey found 51% of tax and finance functions early in data maturity.
approach: Tax owns or co-owns a central store fed from several systems, with documented lineage and reconciliations; Snowflake, Fortive and Apple advertise roles.
Deloitte Tax and Databricks announced an alliance on 2025-10-08 to build a unified tax data architecture. No outcomes published.
Tax staff review reconciliations, IT and tax agree ERP changes, and tax leadership signs off data requirements for new business lines.

title: Agentic layer that assembles, maps and checks ledger data before tax engines
problem: Commentators argue data assembly and reconciliation, not tax calculation, is the binding constraint; EY says tax staff spend 53% of time on routine activities.
approach: An agentic layer pulls ledger data, maps accounts to tax categories, validates it, flags anomalies for a person and passes it on.
Kognitos positions its product this way; Thomson Reuters says its goal for ONESOURCE direct tax is agentic data import, validation and mapping.
A person reviews every flagged exception, and tax professionals keep oversight of mapped data. No outcomes published.

title: Agent keeps tax-engine settings in sync with ERP master-data changes
problem: New entities, registrations, locations and products set up in the ERP must be duplicated in the tax engine, and manual maintenance causes mismatches and delays.
approach: Vertex Configuration Agent for Microsoft Dynamics 365 monitors master-data changes and triggers matching updates in the Vertex tax engine.
Vertex says it was built with Azure AI Foundry and Copilot Studio; Avalara describes a browser agent guiding ERP configuration.
The tax team validates high-impact configuration changes before they reach the engine. No outcome figures published.

title: Building tax data and tax engine into ERP migration from the start
problem: Tax determination is often overlooked until late in an ERP project, causing delays and workarounds; one participant managed tax across 40 separate billing systems.
approach: Put a tax expert on the migration team, clean data before it moves, and integrate the tax engine natively.
At Vertex Exchange Europe 2026, Siemens Energy and Daimler Truck AG described implementing the Vertex tax engine in SAP.
Roundtable participants used AI for contract review and anomaly detection, warning it needs clean data. A tax expert sits on the team.

title: Low-code tax data preparation, the pre-generative-AI baseline
problem: Large tax departments gather data from scattered sources by hand before provision and return work can begin; at one telecom client 200-plus tax managers worked above capacity.
approach: Not generative AI: Alteryx and Microsoft Power Query consolidate and reconcile data and feed tax engines; DuPont combined Alteryx with ONESOURCE.
RGP reports 1,100+ hours removed at an automotive client; Concentrix reports 500+ hours a year saved at a telecom client (vendor-published).
Concentrix says any reviewer can verify the visual workflows; no review step is described.

title: Plain-language tax analytics and reusable tax agents over a semantic layer
problem: Tax analysts work in spreadsheets and filings, and refreshing dashboards by hand takes time that could go to analysis and exception handling.
approach: Snowflake's tax analytics team says it replaced traditional dashboards with AI agents, semantic models for plain-English queries, and Streamlit apps.
The posting asks for verified-query coverage and accuracy iteration based on evaluation metrics. No outcomes published.
The builder validates the output; tax leadership receives summaries and owns exception handling.

title: Tax analysts build pipelines and tools with AI coding, under controls
problem: Data integrations tax needs can wait months in an IT queue, and building them fast lets an analyst deploy something nobody has reviewed or documented.
approach: Tax analysts use AI coding and low-code agent tools to build pipelines and apps; four OpenAI tax staff demonstrated pipelines at TEI.
The recap author describes about 15 minutes versus about two months in an IT queue (self-reported, anecdotal).
Any pipeline is reviewed and documented before it is relied on; the recap names unreviewed pipelines as the failure mode.

title: Tax automations run as controlled assets with sign-off, logs and drift monitoring
problem: Under SOX, tax teams must document what an automated process ran, when it changed and who approved it, but most workflow tools lack native run history.
approach: Savant's Spring 2026 release added version control, a sign-off step enforcing segregation of duties, and evidence logs with SOX report templates.
Oxford Industries' senior director of tax and accounting is quoted saying Savant provided the governance controls and audit documentation needed.
A control owner approves before go-live, exceptions go to human review, and drift signals trigger accuracy evaluations.

title: Scheduled multi-system tax reconciliation with exceptions sent to staff
problem: Month-end sales tax reconciliation between source transactions, tax-engine output and returns is done in manual spreadsheets.
approach: Rover, a pet-care marketplace, rebuilt its monthly reconciliation in Savant: it pulls data including Avalara, matches transactions and produces audit-ready outputs.
Rover cut month-end close time 80% and data handling costs 50% (vendor-published).
Human checkpoints are not described for Rover; Savant says exceptions can be routed for human review.

title: Idea: multi-agent workflows from provision to return, people handling exceptions
problem: Idea, not a deployment: a TEI-SJSU panel deck says without an orchestration layer AI cannot move from demo to production, and fragmented data leaves tools isolated.
approach: The panel deck (RSM, Grant Thornton, EY, OpenAI speakers) places multi-agent tax workflows at the top of a four-step progression.
Its examples include provision-to-return automation, R&D credit scanning and state apportionment data ingestion.
Humans are reserved for exceptions.

title: AI extraction of tax notices and documents into structured data, independently verified
problem: State tax notices never arrive in the same format twice, and incorrect document extraction creates errors that flow silently into a return.
approach: TEI attendees reported using AI image-to-text tools on state notices; EY describes AI that summarises a notice and drafts a response.
Savant's Spring 2026 release has over ten prebuilt extraction skills; Avalara's Outlook agent scans inbound invoices and validates them.
Extracted figures are independently verified against source documents, with escalation for complex cases. No error rate published.

title: Transaction-level real-time reporting to tax authorities replaces periodic returns
problem: Periodic returns give authorities data weeks after the transaction; more than 60 jurisdictions have moved or are moving to continuous transaction controls.
approach: Companies send invoice data to the authority as it is created and build around it; the EU adopted ViDA on 2025-03-11.
Commission projects up to EUR 11 billion a year less VAT fraud (independent; unmeasured); a Peru study found over 5% higher reports.
Human checkpoints are not described for in-house teams.
who: European Commission, OECD forum, UK government

title: Invoice and master data validated before submission, with preventive controls
problem: In clearance regimes an invoice has no legal force until the authority returns its identifier, so a wrong VAT ID or schema gets it rejected.
approach: Tax, finance and IT run a validation layer over ERP invoice data, checking identifiers, schema and master data, with an exception queue.
TEI attendees described validation agents critiquing their own outputs, without naming a company or saying they target outbound invoices.
Sources describe no human checkpoint; only 22% of respondents have a formal ViDA transition programme (vendor-published baseline).

title: AI mapping of ERP data to e-invoicing formats, with fixes after approval
problem: A wrong VAT ID or mismatched master data means a clearance-regime invoice is rejected, the shipment waits and the buyer does not pay.
approach: Avalara says it uses AI to map invoice fields to country requirements; Sovos describes AI that diagnoses and fixes errors once approved.
Sovos reports a 1.6% invoice rejection rate in live French production versus an estimated 20% market-wide (vendor-published; AI share unstated).
User approval is required before a correction is executed.

title: Agent assesses rule changes and errors against tax configuration, fixing after approval
problem: Rule and format changes must be mapped to each company's entities and settings, and fixing configuration errors depends on support tickets and hand-offs.
approach: Sovos announced (March 2026) Sovi AI diagnosing compliance errors, proposing fixes and executing corrections once approved, plus regulatory intelligence on configuration impact.
EY's author describes agents that monitor rule changes and route exceptions; the text says EY's platform aims to work this way.
Corrections run only after user approval; exceptions are routed for review. No outcomes published.

title: Idea: continuous reconciliation of calculated, invoiced, reported and authority data
problem: Idea, not a deployment: where authorities hold structured transaction data, indirect tax teams must show what was calculated is what was invoiced and reported.
approach: Reconcile every transaction across calculation, invoice, report and authority record continuously, toward continuous audit controls discussed at Vertex Exchange Europe 2026.
Deloitte's scenario describes a digital tax analyst agent that cross-checks invoice data and routes exceptions to reviewers.
Exceptions go to the appropriate human reviewer.

title: Read-only access lets general AI assistants answer from company tax-compliance data
problem: Staff must log in to a compliance portal to see nexus, filings and registrations, and generic assistants answer from general knowledge, not company numbers.
approach: Kintsugi's MCP server gives Claude or ChatGPT read-only access to nexus, filings and registrations; Avalara and Anrok describe similar servers.
Anrok says its server can also take actions, under scoped OAuth credentials. No outcomes published.
Kintsugi's assistant answers questions only; filings remain checked by the vendor's experts.

title: Company agents call tax engines through vendor servers, limited scopes, logged
problem: Each AI model and tax system needs custom integration, and calling a tax engine from an agent raises questions of authorisation, identity and logging.
approach: Avalara says it ships MCP servers for AvaTax, returns and e-invoicing; an example agent validates a vendor invoice and files use tax.
Sovos is developing an MCP gateway; Vertex's Dynamics 365 agent and PwC's Agent OS use MCP. No named customer outcomes.
Users consent to permissions and consents are audited; Vertex keeps review checkpoints for high-impact changes.

title: Decision log and audit trail for AI-assisted tax determinations and approvals
problem: Fonoa's 2026 survey of 176 indirect tax leaders found 57.4% would not be confident defending AI-assisted decisions to a tax authority.
approach: Record which AI outputs affected filings, the inputs used, and which suggestions were accepted, modified or rejected, as work happens.
Fonoa markets an Audit product claiming audit-ready 'in minutes, not weeks' (vendor claim, no sample); Sovos says every approval is documented.
Formal human review of AI output before it informs a decision, with named owners and documented sign-off.

title: Tax-owned AI and automation inventory, policy and accountability
problem: When TEI seminar attendees were asked whether tax owns AI implementation, two hands went up out of more than 50.
approach: Tax keeps a live inventory of AI and automation use cases with owners and escalation paths, a written policy and control mapping.
COSO's February 2026 guidance sets a six-step roadmap: govern, inventory, assess, design, implement, monitor.
Each inventoried use case has named ownership and escalation paths. In one report, 45% of tax departments had no relevant policy.

title: Acceptance thresholds before go-live, then tracking accuracy and override rates
problem: Tax functions are told to adopt AI but not what good looks like: only 12.5% of Fonoa's respondents had specific AI targets or KPIs.
approach: Tax sets acceptance thresholds before go-live and monitors accuracy, override rates and cycle time afterwards.
In Deloitte's survey, 77% of tax leaders required 90% or higher accuracy before entrusting AI with tax processes (vendor-published).
Formal human review of AI outputs before they inform tax decisions, run by about a third of Fonoa's respondents.

title: AI-first in-house tax model where staff build and review database-driven workflows
problem: OpenAI's postings describe moving recurring income tax work off spreadsheet preparation and trackers, and making handoffs and documentation easier to review.
approach: OpenAI's tax postings describe an AI-first model where preparation is automated in database-driven workflows and staff review, validate and build.
The team wants a leader who defines when AI can safely speed work and when human review is needed. No outcomes published.
First-level review and validation of automated provision outputs and pipelines.

title: Central tax operations and technology team owning tax data, automation and AI
problem: In the 2026 Thomson Reuters Institute report, 64% placed their tax department at the chaotic or reactive end of a maturity curve, up from 57%.
approach: Set up a central team owning tax technology, data and automation; Unilever Ice Cream's Anna Elphick discussed a centralised tax operations centre.
A German head of tax told EY of a dedicated AI team for tax; Deloitte advises collaborating with finance and IT.
Governance framework with named owners, documented sign-off and internal reviews. Reported correlations are not shown to be causal.
who: Unilever Ice Cream, Thomson Reuters, EY

title: Tax run as co-sourced or managed service on a provider's AI platforms
problem: In-house teams struggle to build their own solutions; 77% wanted their providers to use generative AI, yet 59% were unsure whether their own firms do.
approach: Use a third party investing in AI and data tooling, or a managed service; 78% in EY's survey said it would help.
Deloitte lists a managed service or selective outsourcing as an option; most large Vertex implementations are partner-led.
The business reviews provider output critically and vets AI vendors on data retention and training terms. 85% reported better focus (vendor-published).
who: EY survey, Deloitte, Thomson Reuters, Vertex
